mainEntity.name: Does a tilted dental implant last as long as a straight one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Controlled tilted implant placement, when carefully planned and executed, can achieve comparable long-term outcomes to axially placed implants. Clinical research on techniques such as All-on-4® has demonstrated favourable survival rates for angled implants in appropriately selected patients. However, success is dependent on many individual factors including bone quality, oral hygiene, and prosthetic design. Whether tilted placement is suitable for a specific patient must be assessed individually during a clinical consultation with a dentist experienced in implant dentistry.

mainEntity.name: What happens if an implant is placed at the wrong angle?

acceptedAnswer.text: If an implant is placed at an unfavourable angle not accounted for in the restorative plan, it may result in excessive bending stresses on the implant-bone interface, difficulties in fabricating a natural-looking restoration, or complications with abutment and crown fit. In the long term, this can contribute to marginal bone loss or restoration failure. This is one reason why thorough pre-surgical planning using three-dimensional imaging is an important aspect of modern implant dentistry.

mainEntity.name: Can bone loss affect the angle at which an implant can be placed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Bone resorption following tooth loss can significantly reduce the volume of bone available for implant placement, limiting the angulation options available to the clinician. In some cases, bone grafting procedures may be recommended to restore sufficient bone volume before or alongside implant placement. Your implant dentist will assess your bone levels using radiographic imaging and discuss whether any preparatory procedures may be appropriate for your situation.

mainEntity.name: Is implant angulation visible in the final restoration?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, the final crown or bridge is designed to emerge naturally from the gum line regardless of the underlying implant angle. Custom or angled abutments are used to correct for the implant's angulation, allowing the restoration to appear and function naturally. Experienced restorative planning ensures the aesthetics and bite function are not compromised by the implant angle. Your clinician will discuss what the planned outcome looks like during your treatment planning appointments.

mainEntity.name: How does bruxism (teeth grinding) affect angled implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bruxism generates significant occlusal forces that can place added stress on implants and their restorations. For angled implants, the nature of off-axis loading means that these additional forces may be of particular concern over time. Patients with bruxism who are considering implants are typically advised to have this assessed as part of treatment planning. A custom-fitted occlusal splint (night guard) may be recommended to help manage these forces and support implant longevity. Individual risk must be assessed clinically.

mainEntity.name: What questions should I ask at an implant consultation regarding angulation?

acceptedAnswer.text: At an implant consultation, you may wish to ask: How will my implants be angled and why? Will a CBCT scan be used in planning? Will a surgical guide be used during placement? How will the abutment compensate for the implant angle? What are the expected long-term outcomes for this type of placement? Understanding the reasoning behind your treatment plan helps you make an informed decision. You can also arrange a review directly through our contact page before your consultation.
